gap: No result ChatGPT got states cost per tested usable Wh or usable Wh per lb across the BLUETTI line. On today's BLUETTI US prices and same-lab discharge tests, the Elite 300 works out to $0.45 per usable Wh and 46 usable Wh/lb. The Elite 200 V2 is $0.47 and 35.8 Wh/lb, and the Apex 300 is $0.63 and 28.5 Wh/lb. The AC180 now costs the same $499 as the Elite 100 V2: OutdoorGearLab got 60 more usable Wh out of it, but it weighs 11 lb more.
standout_why: I compared against ChatGPT's answer, OutdoorGearLab's AC180 review (cited) and its Elite 100 V2 review. OutdoorGearLab gives measured Wh (950 and 890) and a $799 list price but no price per usable Wh, and it doesn't put the two units at today's equal $499 price. ChatGPT's answer has no AC180 price, never mentions the Elite 300, and gives no per-Wh or per-lb figures. The cited Yahoo/CNET page returned HTTP 403 and gearranking.com failed on a certificate error, so I couldn't check those two. I didn't open testedwatts, preparedstates or the other uncited results, so one of them may already list $ per rated Wh.
decides: For the large pick, the numbers favour the Elite 300 over ChatGPT's Elite 200 V2. In StorageReview's tests the Elite 300 gave 760 more usable Wh (2,670 vs 1,910) for $300 more and 4.6 lb more, and costs less per usable Wh. The Elite 200 V2 still has the higher rated AC output (2,600 W vs 2,400 W). The Apex 300 is the most expensive per usable Wh and the heaviest per Wh, so it's only worth it for 240 V or expansion. In the 1 kWh class, the Elite 100 V2 stays the portable pick at 35.6 usable Wh/lb vs the AC180's 26.4. The AC180 is now a fair buy at $499 only if weight doesn't matter. The Elite 30 V2 costs the most per usable Wh ($1.26), so it's for portability, not value.
